ocar.opportunity: Cells compartmentalize thousands of proteins, yet how those proteins sit relative to whole-cell ultrastructure is still poorly mapped. Correlative super-resolution fluorescence and electron microscopy can place named proteins inside a global structural context.
ocar.challenge: Prior correlative imaging traded off ultrastructure preservation, fluorescence retention, sensitivity, resolution, and field of view, so protein-ultrastructure relationships across entire cells remained speculative.
ocar.action: Hoffman, Betzig, Hess and colleagues froze fluorescently labeled cultured mammalian cells in vitreous ice, imaged selected cells entirely below 10 K by multicolor 3D structured illumination and single-molecule localization microscopy, then imaged the same cells by focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy at 4- or 8-nm isotropic resolution and registered the volumes.
ocar.resolution: The registered volumes revealed unexpected relationships, including endoplasmic-reticulum-marker-positive intranuclear vesicles, size-dependent peroxisome shape, highly convoluted endolysosomes, a web-like adhesion network between cerebellar granule neurons, and chromatin domains subclassified by transcriptional-activity markers. Two-color cryo localization microscopy supported whole-cell registration quantified to about 40 nm.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the pipeline as a hypothesis generator for biochemistry in a spatially compartmentalized cell and for studying natural cell-to-cell variability while preserving native ultrastructure.

summaries.beginner: It is hard to see both a cell’s fine inner architecture and where specific proteins sit, all at once, across an entire cell. This team froze whole cultured cells, took a protein map and a detailed structural map of the same cells, and lined the two pictures up.
summaries.intermediate: In Science in 2019, Hoffman and colleagues combined cryogenic super-resolution fluorescence microscopy with focused ion beam block-face electron microscopy of entire vitreously frozen mammalian cells. Independent optimization of the light and electron steps, followed by nanoscale registration, let them segment crowded organelles and report unexpected protein-ultrastructure pairings, including web-like adhesions between cultured cerebellar granule neurons. The work sits at the image-acquisition stage of volumetric reconstruction rather than as a tissue connectome.
summaries.advanced: Findings are from cultured mammalian cells, not reconstructed neural circuits in tissue. FIB-SEM sampling is 4 or 8 nm isotropic; cryo localization registration is quantified to about 40 nm, coarser than either modality’s finest local scale. Observations are framed as hypothesis-generating ultrastructural variability, not a complete protein census. Catalog methods are FIB-SEM and super-resolution light microscopy.

plain_language_summary: It is hard to see both a cell’s fine inner architecture and where specific proteins sit, all at once, across an entire cell. This team froze whole cultured cells, took a protein map and a detailed structural map of the same cells, and lined the two pictures up.

ocar.opportunity: As microscopy volumes reach terabytes, the integer label volumes that store segment identities become enormous as well. Fast queries that ask which segments occupy a region are essential for empty-space skipping in rendering and for spatial proximity searches.
ocar.challenge: Integer label data are harder to store and randomly access than raw images, especially when millions of segments must be culled quickly without loading entire volumes.
ocar.action: Beyer and colleagues introduce a label list tree that adaptively stores each spatial region with either a probabilistic constant-time representation for conservative culling or a deterministic logarithmic-time representation for exact queries, plus a query-adaptive strategy that prunes queries while descending the tree.
ocar.resolution: On large connectomics volumes, including a brain scan with more than 13 million labeled segments, the hybrid structure reduced storage and improved query times relative to conventional culling.
ocar.future_work: The comparison is to conventional culling on several large datasets; extending the same adaptive encoding to other label-heavy visualization tasks is a natural next use.

summaries.beginner: Huge 3D maps of cells create equally huge lists of which cell is where. This paper describes a faster way to look up which labeled objects sit in a given region so computers can draw or search the maps quickly.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics in 2019, Beyer, Pfister, Hadwiger and colleagues targeted integer segmentation volumes from terabyte-scale microscopy. Their label list tree mixes probabilistic constant-time culling with exact logarithmic-time queries and chooses representations per region and per query. They report storage and speed gains on connectomics data, including a scan with more than 13 million segments.
summaries.advanced: The method is a visualization and query data structure, not a segmentation algorithm. Reported gains are relative to conventional culling; the abstract does not specify which production connectome the 13-million-segment scan is. Probabilistic nodes are conservative, so exactness is not uniform across the tree.

plain_language_summary: Huge 3D maps of cells create equally huge lists of which cell is where. This paper describes a faster way to look up which labeled objects sit in a given region so computers can draw or search the maps quickly.

ocar.opportunity: Ongoing projects are mapping connectomes, but full physiological response properties of every neuron remain out of reach. Theory can ask how much of a circuit’s computation can be ruled out from structure alone.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear how far a wiring diagram advances mechanistic understanding when high-level function is unknown and neuron response properties are unconstrained.
ocar.action: Building on prior theory of connectomic constraints for feedforward deterministic spiking networks, Ramaswamy studies the space of spike-train to spike-train transformations, relates architecture classes to hierarchical subsets of that space, and proves lower bounds even when the smallest containing subset cannot be identified exactly.
ocar.resolution: After making the framework precise, the paper constructs explicit hierarchy classes and proves several such lower bounds on which transformations feedforward-like architectures can realize.
ocar.future_work: The program is theoretical; applying the bounds to specific mapped connectomes and to architectures beyond the feedforward setting is left open.

summaries.beginner: Having a wiring diagram of a brain does not automatically tell you what the circuit computes, because we often cannot measure every cell’s electrical personality. This theory paper asks what computations can be ruled out from structure alone.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv in 2019, Ramaswamy extends a theory of connectomic constraints for feedforward networks of axiomatic deterministic spiking neurons. Rather than simulating a particular animal, the work studies the space of spike-train transformations and proves lower bounds on which hierarchical subsets can contain the maps realized by given architecture classes. The intended use is to bound what a connectome can and cannot compute when physiology is unknown.
summaries.advanced: Neurons are abstract objects obeying a small axiom set, not biophysically detailed models. The setting is feedforward-like transformations; recurrent dynamics and stochastic synapses are outside the stated results. No empirical connectome is analyzed. Catalog stage is infrastructure.

plain_language_summary: Having a wiring diagram of a brain does not automatically tell you what the circuit computes, because we often cannot measure every cell’s electrical personality. This theory paper asks what computations can be ruled out from structure alone.

ocar.opportunity: The fly optic lobe tiles roughly 800 stereotyped columnar microcircuits. Specializations of those columns, such as the dorsal rim area that detects linearly polarized skylight, can reveal how photoreceptor identity is wired into orientation behavior.
ocar.challenge: Differences in cellular composition and synaptic connectivity among functionally specialized columns remained largely unknown.
ocar.action: Sancer, Wernet and colleagues mapped medulla columns downstream of dorsal-rim photoreceptors, identified previously uncharacterized Dm cell types, tested connections with activity-dependent GRASP and trans-Tango, and live-imaged pupal photoreceptor axons as they reached layer M6.
ocar.resolution: Only in dorsal-rim medulla columns do both R7 and R8 target the bona fide R7 layer and contact modality-specific Dm-DRA1 and Dm-DRA2 cells that avoid color-sensitive Dm8 arbors. DRA R7 synapses onto Dm-DRA1 and DRA R8 onto Dm-DRA2; the two photoreceptor classes arrive at M6 sequentially. The authors propose a duplicated R7-to-Dm circuit as an adaptation for orthogonal e-vector analysis.
ocar.future_work: The preprint frames this architecture as an ideal specialization for polarized skylight; how the same motif operates in behaving adults is not resolved here.

summaries.beginner: Flies can use the sky’s polarized light as a compass. This paper maps the special visual columns that handle that signal and shows they are wired differently from ordinary color-sensing columns.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2019 bioRxiv preprint, Sancer, Wernet and colleagues describe medulla circuitry downstream of Drosophila dorsal-rim photoreceptors. They report two dorsal-rim-specific Dm types that stratify in separate sublayers and contact only polarization-sensitive R7 and R8 inputs, confirmed with GRASP and trans-Tango, and they show sequential arrival of those photoreceptor terminals at layer M6. The proposed function is duplicated R7-like analyzers for orthogonal e-vectors.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint. Functional tests are GRASP and trans-Tango rather than full physiology of orientation behavior. Catalog fields list no dataset or organism tags, but the title and abstract are fly visual system. Sequential axon arrival is from pupal live imaging, not adult dynamics.

plain_language_summary: Flies can use the sky’s polarized light as a compass. This paper maps the special visual columns that handle that signal and shows they are wired differently from ordinary color-sensing columns.

ocar.opportunity: Modulatory neurons supply teaching signals for associative learning, but the circuits that compute those signals are poorly known. A complete upstream connectome of mushroom-body modulators would show how memories can regulate later learning.
ocar.challenge: Which sensory afferents and recurrent pathways control dopaminergic and other modulatory neurons in a compact learning center had not been reconstructed at synaptic resolution.
ocar.action: Eschbach, Zlatic, Cardona and colleagues reconstructed the circuitry upstream of all modulatory neurons in the Drosophila larva mushroom body, functionally tested some pathways, and built a connectome-constrained model of learning performance.
ocar.resolution: They report afferent sensory paths plus 61 feedback neuron pairs providing one- and two-step feedback from mushroom-body output neurons, many linking aversive and appetitive memory systems. Some modulators compare inhibition from their own compartment with excitation from opposite-valence compartments. The model indicates that multilevel feedback and cross-compartment connections increase computational flexibility.
ocar.future_work: The authors present this as a detailed view of a recurrent teaching-signal circuit; broader tests of the model’s predicted learning tasks remain a next step.

summaries.beginner: When an animal learns that a smell predicts a reward or a punishment, special teaching cells change the strength of connections. This paper maps who talks to those teaching cells in a young fruit fly and how leftover memories can change what is learned next.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv in 2019, Eschbach and colleagues provide a synaptic-resolution connectome upstream of all modulatory neurons in the Drosophila larva mushroom body, using the larval EM volume. They describe 61 feedback neuron pairs, extensive cross-talk between aversive and appetitive compartments, and functional confirmation that some modulators integrate opposite-valence inputs. A constrained model argues that these motifs improve learning-task performance.
summaries.advanced: The reconstruction is larval, not adult, mushroom body. Functional confirmation covers some, not all, structural pathways. Teaching-signal computation is inferred from connectivity plus a subset of physiology and a model, not a full behavioral screen of every motif. Catalog dataset is DS03 Drosophila larva.

plain_language_summary: When an animal learns that a smell predicts a reward or a punishment, special teaching cells change the strength of connections. This paper maps who talks to those teaching cells in a young fruit fly and how leftover memories can change what is learned next.

ocar.opportunity: Müller glia are first to show metabolic and morphological stress in retinal degeneration, so reconstructing them in a pathoconnectome can link glial change to neighboring neurons and other glia.
ocar.challenge: How chaotic Müller-cell metabolic shifts relate to neuronal stress, synapse maintenance, or glia-glia interactions in early remodeling was unknown.
ocar.action: Pfeiffer, Jones and colleagues reconstruct a Müller cell from retinal pathoconnectome 1 (RPC1), combining ultrastructure with computational molecular phenotyping of small-molecule metabolites.
ocar.resolution: They find intra- and intercellular variation in osmication intensity, variation in Müller-cell metabolite content, and morphological changes at glial endfeet, providing a framework to score neural-glial interactions in early remodeling.
ocar.future_work: RPC1 is positioned as a starting reconstruction for relating structure and metabolism as degeneration proceeds.

summaries.beginner: When a retina begins to degenerate, support cells called Müller glia change first. This study rebuilds one of those cells in three dimensions and looks at its chemistry next to nearby neurons.
summaries.intermediate: In Advances in Experimental Medicine and Biology in 2019, Pfeiffer, Marc, Jones and colleagues reconstruct a Müller cell from mouse retinal pathoconnectome 1. Using electron microscopy plus computational molecular phenotyping, they report variable osmication, heterogeneous small-molecule content, and altered endfeet in early remodeling. The chapter argues this resolution can link glial phenotype to neuronal and glial neighbors.
summaries.advanced: The reconstruction is a single Müller cell in an early-remodeling pathoconnectome, not a population census. Causal links among metabolism, synapses, and stress are not established. Catalog dataset is DS09/DS10 mouse retina.

plain_language_summary: When a retina begins to degenerate, support cells called Müller glia change first. This study rebuilds one of those cells in three dimensions and looks at its chemistry next to nearby neurons.

ocar.opportunity: Complete three-dimensional neuron shape is a core cell-type feature, but whole-brain reconstruction of long-projecting mammalian neurons requires handling tens of teravoxels and laborious validation.
ocar.challenge: Complex arbors and long axons make precise tracing and collaborative checking extremely costly in huge light-microscopy brains.
ocar.action: Wang, Peng and colleagues develop TeraVR, an open-source virtual-reality annotation system with immersive collaborative visualization and hierarchical streaming of teravoxel-scale images.
ocar.resolution: Using TeraVR they report precise full morphologies of long-projecting neurons in whole mouse brains and a collaborative workflow aimed at high-accuracy reconstruction.
ocar.future_work: The system is released to support broader production of whole-brain neuronal shapes from similarly large image volumes.

summaries.beginner: A mouse neuron can send a branch across the whole brain, and the pictures of that brain are enormous. This paper offers a virtual-reality tool so people can trace those complete shapes more accurately together.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications in 2019, Wang, Peng, Zeng and colleagues introduce TeraVR, an open-source VR annotation platform for teravoxel whole-brain images. Hierarchical streaming and collaborative 3D interaction are used to reconstruct complete morphologies of long-projecting mouse neurons. The claim is improved precision and a practical multi-user workflow, not a new imaging modality.
summaries.advanced: TeraVR is a proofreading and annotation interface; accuracy claims are qualitative in the abstract. Catalog organism is mouse; no registry EM volume is attached. Whole-brain here refers to light-microscopy morphology, not a synaptic connectome.

plain_language_summary: A mouse neuron can send a branch across the whole brain, and the pictures of that brain are enormous. This paper offers a virtual-reality tool so people can trace those complete shapes more accurately together.

ocar.opportunity: Synapses are numerous and molecularly complex; mapping synaptic protein combinations across an entire mouse brain could reveal how synapse types tile anatomy and relate to circuits and behavior.
ocar.challenge: Examining proteins in individual excitatory synapses in all regions, at a scale that yields a brain-wide catalog, required new genetic labeling and imaging methods.
ocar.action: Zhu, Grant and colleagues developed labeling and imaging to measure molecular and morphological features of excitatory synapses across mouse brain regions, generating synapse catalogs they term a synaptome.
ocar.resolution: They report unique anatomical distributions for synapse subtypes, region-specific subtype signatures, correspondence with structural and functional connectomes, activity-triggered postsynaptic responses that depend on synaptome maps, greatest diversity in higher cognitive areas, and reorganization of maps by mutations causing cognitive disorders. Catalogs were generated from features of a billion synapses.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the technology and resources as widely applicable to normal and diseased brain studies.

summaries.beginner: The brain’s connections are not all the same: synapses come in many molecular flavors. This paper maps those flavors across the mouse brain and shows that different regions, and some disease mutations, rearrange the mix.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron in 2018, Zhu, Grant and colleagues genetically label synaptic proteins and image individual excitatory synapses across mouse brain regions, compiling catalogs from molecular and morphological features of a billion synapses. They argue each subtype has a characteristic anatomy, that synaptome maps align with connectomes, and that cognitive areas are most diverse. Mutations linked to cognitive disorders reorganized the maps.
summaries.advanced: The resource is a molecular/morphological synaptome of excitatory synapses, not an electron-microscopy connectome. ‘A billion synapses’ is a catalog scale stated in the abstract; sampling density per region is not specified here. Causal claims about behavior rest on activity patterns and mutant maps as reported, not on a full circuit reconstruction.

plain_language_summary: The brain’s connections are not all the same: synapses come in many molecular flavors. This paper maps those flavors across the mouse brain and shows that different regions, and some disease mutations, rearrange the mix.

ocar.opportunity: Central pattern generators create motor rhythm; in C. elegans, identifying which cells oscillate would compress sensorimotor function into a numerically small nervous system.
ocar.challenge: The origin of body-undulation rhythm during forward versus reverse movement was not settled.
ocar.action: Wen, Gao and Zhen review and synthesize recent findings on ventral-cord excitatory motor neurons as intrinsic oscillators, proprioceptive coupling, and descending premotor innervation.
ocar.resolution: They propose that A-class and mid-body B-class excitatory motor neurons act as non-bursting intrinsic oscillators for reversal and forward undulation, that proprioception phase-couples members of a class, and that distinct premotor pools modulate oscillations and bidirectional coupling. Integrating rhythm generation and proprioception into motor neurons, and descending regulation into premotor interneurons, yields a compressed analogue of more complex systems.
ocar.future_work: The article is part of a meeting issue on cellular-resolution C. elegans modeling and calls for a mechanistic, dynamic sensorimotor model built on this circuit sketch.

summaries.beginner: Tiny roundworms swim by bending in waves, but it was unclear which nerve cells keep the beat. This review argues that certain motor neurons along the body can generate the rhythm themselves and pass it along as the animal moves forward or backward.
summaries.intermediate: In Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B in 2018, Wen, Gao and Zhen discuss evidence that C. elegans A- and mid-body B-class excitatory ventral-cord motor neurons are non-bursting intrinsic oscillators for reverse and forward undulation. Proprioception entrains and phase-couples same-class cells, while premotor interneurons modulate oscillation and coupling. The authors frame this as functional compression in a compact nervous system.
summaries.advanced: This is a review/synthesis, not a new connectome. Catalog datasets include DS01 C. elegans and DS07 VNC (FANC/MANC) with organism tags elegans and fly; the scientific argument in the abstract is C. elegans motor rhythm. Oscillator claims are attributed to recent findings under discussion rather than a single new experiment in this paper.

plain_language_summary: Tiny roundworms swim by bending in waves, but it was unclear which nerve cells keep the beat. This review argues that certain motor neurons along the body can generate the rhythm themselves and pass it along as the animal moves forward or backward.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans body waves are confined to a dorso-ventral plane, but the snout can explore in all directions, a likely advantage in soil. Head innervation may explain those extra degrees of freedom.
ocar.challenge: The neural basis of three-dimensional snout exploration, as opposed to planar locomotion, needed a circuit-level anatomical account.
ocar.action: White compares muscle innervation along the body versus the snout and relates octant-specific motor, sensory, and interneurons to exploratory movements.
ocar.resolution: Body muscle quadrants share dorsal or ventral innervation, whereas snout muscles have an octagonal innervation layout. Exploratory snout behavior is likely mediated by octant-specific neurons. The defined anatomy is proposed as a substrate for models of foraging-like exploration.
ocar.future_work: The paper argues that this structure plus behavioral observations should enable models of the neural basis of snout exploration.

summaries.beginner: A roundworm’s body mostly bends up and down, but its nose can poke around in every direction. This essay uses the wiring of head muscles to explain how that extra freedom might work.
summaries.intermediate: In Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B in 2018, J. White contrasts dorso-ventral body wave constraints with multi-axis snout exploration in C. elegans. Shared innervation of dorsal versus ventral muscle quadrants along the body is set against octagonal snout innervation. Octant-specific motor, sensory, and interneurons are proposed to mediate soil-like exploratory movements.
summaries.advanced: This is an anatomical and conceptual contribution in a modeling meeting issue, not a new EM reconstruction. Causal control of exploration is inferred from somatotopy and is explicitly framed as a modeling opportunity. Catalog dataset is DS01 C. elegans.

plain_language_summary: A roundworm’s body mostly bends up and down, but its nose can poke around in every direction. This essay uses the wiring of head muscles to explain how that extra freedom might work.

ocar.opportunity: Eigenvectors of networks highlight well-connected vertices; extending that idea to communities attached to prominent nodes could expose information hubs from static graphs.
ocar.challenge: It was often assumed that static connectomes cannot reveal dynamic information-flow hubs the way numerical simulations can.
ocar.action: Clark and Macdonald define eigenvector-based communities, each associated with a prominent vertex, and apply the method to C. elegans, macaque, and a large-scale human MRI connectome of about 1.8 million vertices.
ocar.resolution: Known C. elegans circuitry appears as separate communities; in macaque the hippocampus emerges as an information hub; in human data, prominent pathways during an MRI scan can match a subject across sessions. The authors argue static graphs can yield insights previously attributed only to flow simulations.
ocar.future_work: Subject identification via matching pathways is demonstrated as a possible unique identifier; broader validation across datasets is implied rather than completed here.

summaries.beginner: Some brain regions act like busy junctions for messages. This paper uses a math trick on wiring diagrams to find those junctions in a worm, a monkey, and human brain scans.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv in 2018, Clark and Macdonald expand eigenvector methods to detect communities tied to prominent nodes and thereby analyze information-flow structure. Applied to C. elegans, macaque, and a human connectome of about 1.8 million vertices, the approach recovers known worm circuits, flags the macaque hippocampus as a hub, and matches human subjects by shared prominent pathways. They contest the view that only dynamic models can reveal such hubs.
summaries.advanced: The human analysis is an MRI-scale connectome, not synaptic EM. ‘Information hub’ is an eigenvector-community interpretation of a static graph. Catalog dataset is DS01 C. elegans; macaque and human applications are additional. Subject-identification claims rest on pathway overlap counts stated in the abstract, without reported accuracy metrics here.

plain_language_summary: Some brain regions act like busy junctions for messages. This paper uses a math trick on wiring diagrams to find those junctions in a worm, a monkey, and human brain scans.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomic electron-microscopy volumes can also reveal mitochondrial morphology linked to disease, but petabyte scale rules out manual annotation.
ocar.challenge: Detectors must be both accurate and faster than modern microscope acquisition if mitochondria are to be mapped in real time.
ocar.action: Casser, Pfister, Haehn and colleagues train a modified U-Net as a fully automatic mitochondria detector and evaluate it on multiple connectomics datasets, including an improved EPFL Hippocampus mitochondria benchmark.
ocar.resolution: They report a Jaccard index of up to 0.90 and inference below 16 ms for a 512×512 tile, faster than modern EM acquisition. Among real-time methods they rank first and third overall versus prior work. Data, results, and code are released.
ocar.future_work: Real-time detection is positioned to keep pace with acquisition; extending the same speed-accuracy tradeoff to other organelles is left open.

summaries.beginner: Tiny energy compartments inside cells, mitochondria, change shape in some diseases, but brain electron-microscope pictures are far too big to outline by hand. This paper trains a computer to find mitochondria fast enough to keep up with the microscope.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2018 arXiv paper, Casser, Kang, Pfister and Haehn present a modified U-Net mitochondria detector for connectomics EM. On several real-world volumes, including an improved EPFL Hippocampus benchmark, they report Jaccard up to 0.90 and sub-16 ms inference on 512×512 tiles. They rank the detector first among real-time methods and third overall, with public code.
summaries.advanced: Jaccard 0.90 is an upper reported value, not a guarantee on every volume. Ranking is among methods considered in the paper. Catalog stages include acquisition, segmentation, and graph analysis; the contribution is segmentation speed. Disease links are motivational, not a clinical evaluation.

plain_language_summary: Tiny energy compartments inside cells, mitochondria, change shape in some diseases, but brain electron-microscope pictures are far too big to outline by hand. This paper trains a computer to find mitochondria fast enough to keep up with the microscope.

ocar.opportunity: A functional connectome that captures how stimuli propagate would complement anatomical wiring, especially in C. elegans where a generative neural-response model exists.
ocar.challenge: Turning high-dimensional neuronal time series into a causal graphical model of the full network is nontrivial.
ocar.action: Liu, Kim and Shlizerman collect simulated neuronal responses, project them with singular value decomposition, extract dominant pairwise dependencies, and build a probabilistic graphical model of the C. elegans somatic nervous system.
ocar.resolution: The resulting PGM represents stimulus-to-neuron causal dependencies, recovers known behavioral pathways, and suggests pathways for novel scenarios.
ocar.future_work: The meeting-issue paper presents the method as a way to obtain and verify pathways; applying it to experimental rather than model-generated traces is a natural extension.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram shows who can talk to whom; a functional map shows who actually influences whom when a signal arrives. This paper turns simulated worm-brain activity into such a functional map.
summaries.intermediate: In Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B in 2018, Liu, Kim and Shlizerman convert neuronal time series into a probabilistic graphical model via SVD projections and pairwise dependencies. Applied to a model of the C. elegans somatic nervous system, the functional connectome recovers known behavioral pathways and proposes others. The work is aimed at causal stimulus propagation rather than new anatomy.
summaries.advanced: Validation uses a generative model of C. elegans responses, not new in vivo recordings. Pairwise dependencies from low-dimensional projections can miss higher-order interactions. Catalog dataset is DS01 C. elegans.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram shows who can talk to whom; a functional map shows who actually influences whom when a signal arrives. This paper turns simulated worm-brain activity into such a functional map.

ocar.opportunity: Presynaptic communication needs energy and calcium buffering, jobs mitochondria are well suited for, and mitochondria are actively recruited to many—but not all—presynapses.
ocar.challenge: How synapses with versus without mitochondria differ, and what extra presynaptic jobs mitochondria perform, remained incompletely synthesized, including implications for disease.
ocar.action: Devine and Kittler review the importance of presynaptic mitochondria for neuronal homeostasis and how their dysfunction might contribute to disease.
ocar.resolution: The review discusses energy supply, calcium buffering, and additional emerging presynaptic mitochondrial functions, and contrasts mitochondria-containing and mitochondria-lacking terminals.
ocar.future_work: The authors highlight disease contribution as an open mechanistic question rather than a settled causal map.

summaries.beginner: Nerve endings need fuel and a way to handle calcium bursts when they send messages. This review explains how mitochondria at those endings help keep neurons healthy and what may go wrong in disease.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Reviews Neuroscience in 2018, Devine and Kittler survey mitochondria at neuronal presynapses. They emphasize energy and calcium buffering, active recruitment to terminals, the fact that not all presynapses contain mitochondria, and additional presynaptic roles, with discussion of disease. It is a field synthesis rather than a methods paper.
summaries.advanced: No new dataset or organism is analyzed. Disease mechanisms are discussed at review depth; the abstract does not quantify prevalence of mitochondria-less terminals. Catalog axis is field_synthesis.

plain_language_summary: Nerve endings need fuel and a way to handle calcium bursts when they send messages. This review explains how mitochondria at those endings help keep neurons healthy and what may go wrong in disease.

ocar.opportunity: Across flies to humans, brain wiring shows heterogeneous connection strengths parsimoniously described by wiring-cost and homophily principles, plus modules and hubs. A developmental mechanism that could generate those adult statistics would unify vertebrate and invertebrate connectomes.
ocar.challenge: How interregional wiring principles and global topology arise was unknown, and typical explanations invoke activity-dependent plasticity or axonal guidance cues.
ocar.action: Goulas, Betzel and Hilgetag use computational modeling of heterochronous, spatially ordered neurodevelopmental gradients without plasticity or guidance cues.
ocar.resolution: The model reconstructs on average 83% of wiring principles and 80% of global network topology across diverse adult connectomes, including fly and human. Space and time are proposed as a parsimonious, potentially universal mechanism.
ocar.future_work: The authors frame the mechanism as plausible and of potential universal scope; testing against additional species and against models that do include guidance cues is implied.

summaries.beginner: Brains of very different animals still seem to follow similar wiring rules, such as keeping long cables costly and grouping similar regions. This modeling study asks whether simple schedules of when and where neurons are born can explain a large share of those adult wiring patterns.
summaries.intermediate: In Science Advances in 2018, Goulas, Betzel and Hilgetag show that heterochronous, spatially ordered developmental gradients, without activity-dependent plasticity or axonal guidance, can reconstruct on average 83% of interregional wiring principles and 80% of global topology in adult connectomes including fly and human. They argue space and time are key components of a parsimonious developmental mechanism. The work is computational rather than a new imaging volume, and the percentages are reconstruction averages for the model, not microscope accuracy.
summaries.advanced: Percentages are model reconstruction averages stated in the abstract, not imaging accuracy. The model omits guidance cues and plasticity by design; residual unexplained structure may require those factors. Catalog stages include proofreading, graph analysis, and modeling; the contribution is computational, not EM proofreading.

plain_language_summary: Brains of very different animals still seem to follow similar wiring rules, such as keeping long cables costly and grouping similar regions. This modeling study asks whether simple schedules of when and where neurons are born can explain a large share of those adult wiring patterns.

ocar.opportunity: To relate nervous-system control to movement, a mechanically realistic C. elegans body with anatomically placed muscles is needed in environments of different viscosity.
ocar.challenge: Linking neural drive to crawling versus swimming requires both an elastic cuticle under hydrostatic pressure and muscle geometry taken from microscopy.
ocar.action: Palyanov, Khayrulin and Larson build a three-dimensional particle-based biomechanical model in Sibernetic using smoothed particle hydrodynamics, with body-wall muscles mapped from light and electron micrographs.
ocar.resolution: Different muscle activation patterns produce crawling and swimming in environments of different viscosities while matching multiple known biomechanical properties of the animal.
ocar.future_work: The meeting-issue paper positions the body model for behavioral analysis once coupled more fully to neural control.

summaries.beginner: To understand how a worm’s nerves move its body, you need a realistic digital body, not just a wiring diagram. This team built a 3D worm that can crawl or swim when its muscles are turned on in different patterns.
summaries.intermediate: In Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B in 2018, Palyanov, Khayrulin and Larson present a Sibernetic smoothed-particle-hydrodynamics model of C. elegans with an elastic cuticle, hydrostatic pressure, and body-wall muscles placed from light and electron microscopy. Varied activation patterns yield crawling and swimming in different viscosities and fit additional known biomechanical properties. Neural drive is imposed as muscle activation patterns rather than a full connectome simulation in this body model.
summaries.advanced: Neural control is imposed as muscle activation patterns, not a full connectome simulation. Catalog method includes electron microscopy for anatomy, not circuit reconstruction. Environmental viscosity is a simulation parameter; quantitative error bars are not in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: To understand how a worm’s nerves move its body, you need a realistic digital body, not just a wiring diagram. This team built a 3D worm that can crawl or swim when its muscles are turned on in different patterns.

ocar.opportunity: Circuit-scale electron microscopy can reconstruct synaptic connectivity of hundreds of neurons in a volume the size of mouse lateral geniculate nucleus, revealing both canonical cell-type wiring and higher-order motifs.
ocar.challenge: Despite well-known core LGN functions, integration of feedforward and feedback, interactions among information channels, and activity-dependent synaptic restructuring remain poorly mapped, especially in mouse LGN as a growing model.
ocar.action: Morgan reviews how cellular connectomics of mouse LGN could address longstanding questions about visual thalamus and mammalian circuit formation.
ocar.resolution: The article argues that intact-network reconstructions can yield cell-type-to-cell-type diagrams plus motifs invisible in pairwise mapping, making LGN a unique testbed for development as well as visual organization.
ocar.future_work: The piece is a prospectus: the connectomic LGN analysis is presented as newly feasible rather than completed in this paper.

summaries.beginner: A way-station in the visual system, the lateral geniculate nucleus, is well studied in outline but still mysterious in its fine wiring. This article explains why mapping every synapse there in a mouse could answer old questions about how visual channels mix and how circuits are built.
summaries.intermediate: In Visual Neuroscience in 2017, Josh Morgan outlines a connectomic program for mouse LGN. Advances in circuit-scale EM make it possible to reconstruct hundreds of neurons in an LGN-sized volume, potentially resolving feedforward/feedback integration, channel interactions, and developmental rewiring. The paper is a conceptual and methodological argument, not a released LGN connectome.
summaries.advanced: No new reconstruction is reported. Catalog organism is mouse and method electron microscopy; claims about what ‘can’ be revealed are prospective. Higher-order motifs require intact networks, so partial volumes may miss them.

plain_language_summary: A way-station in the visual system, the lateral geniculate nucleus, is well studied in outline but still mysterious in its fine wiring. This article explains why mapping every synapse there in a mouse could answer old questions about how visual channels mix and how circuits are built.

ocar.opportunity: Quantifying synaptic vesicles in electron tomograms can compare development and mutants, but manual 3D reconstruction does not scale.
ocar.challenge: Automatic reconstruction must handle crowded vesicle pools while allowing optional human revision of false positives.
ocar.action: Kaltdorf, Stigloher and colleagues implement 3D ART VeSElecT as Fiji macros for registration and measurement, with preprocessing, 3D segmentation, spherical diameter estimates, and RoiManager-based cleanup, applied to zebrafish neuromuscular junctions at 4 and 8 days post-fertilization and to C. elegans N2 versus unc-59(e261) septin mutants.
ocar.resolution: They report development-specific and mutant-specific vesicle-pool changes, smaller vesicles in 8 dpf than 4 dpf zebrafish (validated manually), and analysis of septin-mutant effects on pool formation and size. Speed can be up to 68 times faster than manual annotation, with small error rates; they compare favorably to learning-based segmentation.
ocar.future_work: Automatic and semi-automatic modes plus a tutorial are provided for broader tomogram analysis.

summaries.beginner: Synaptic vesicles are tiny bubbles that store chemical messages, and counting them by hand in 3D microscope movies is slow. This team wrote a Fiji tool that finds vesicles automatically and still lets a person delete mistakes.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Computational Biology in 2017, Kaltdorf, Stigloher and colleagues release 3D ART VeSElecT for electron tomograms. Applied to zebrafish neuromuscular junctions at 4 versus 8 dpf and to C. elegans wild-type versus unc-59(e261), the macros quantify vesicle volume and inner/outer diameter after 3D segmentation. They report smaller vesicles at 8 dpf, mutant pool differences, up to 68-fold speedup versus manual work, and a manual revision step to cut false positives.
summaries.advanced: Speedup ‘up to 68 times’ is a maximum stated in the abstract. Preprocessing assumes stacks at 1 nm/pixel in x and y. Performance metrics include precision/recall and true-versus-detected vesicles; exact numeric error rates beyond ‘small’ are not given here. Catalog datasets are DS01 C. elegans and DS15 zebrafish.

plain_language_summary: Synaptic vesicles are tiny bubbles that store chemical messages, and counting them by hand in 3D microscope movies is slow. This team wrote a Fiji tool that finds vesicles automatically and still lets a person delete mistakes.

ocar.opportunity: A pair of identified serotonergic neurons, the CSDns, can serve as a model for how individual modulatory cells attach to a well-studied olfactory network in Drosophila.
ocar.challenge: Modulatory neurons are morphologically and genetically diverse, so class-level averages hide whether a two-cell system has stereotyped, nonuniform synapses.
ocar.action: Coates, Dacks and colleagues mapped neuronal classes providing input to CSDns in the antennal lobe, quantified CSDn active zones per glomerulus, and tested outputs onto local interneurons, projection neurons, and olfactory receptor neurons.
ocar.resolution: CSDns receive glomerulus-specific input from olfactory receptor and projection neurons and network-wide input from local interneurons, while output is heterogeneous across glomeruli yet stereotyped across animals. They synapse broadly onto local and projection neurons but not onto olfactory receptor neurons. Even a two-cell modulatory network can have highly heterogeneous, stereotyped connectivity that is not purely top-down.
ocar.future_work: The results are offered as a framework for modulatory connectivity more generally.

summaries.beginner: Brain chemicals like serotonin are released by cells that reach many places, so it is easy to imagine they spray the same signal everywhere. This fly study shows that even two identified serotonin cells make a patchy, but repeatable, pattern of contacts in the smell center.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neuroscience in 2017, Coates and colleagues anatomically map inputs and outputs of Drosophila CSDns in the antennal lobe. Inputs are glomerulus-specific from receptor and projection neurons and widespread from local interneurons; active-zone density varies by glomerulus but is stereotyped across animals; outputs hit local and projection neurons, not receptor neurons. Modulation here is not purely descending.
summaries.advanced: Connectivity is anatomical (including active-zone counts), not a full EM connectome of the antennal lobe. Heterogeneity is across glomeruli, not a claim about all serotonergic cells. Catalog organism is fly; stages listed as infrastructure.

plain_language_summary: Brain chemicals like serotonin are released by cells that reach many places, so it is easy to imagine they spray the same signal everywhere. This fly study shows that even two identified serotonin cells make a patchy, but repeatable, pattern of contacts in the smell center.

ocar.opportunity: Functional connectivity inferred from activity could complement electron microscopy if statistical methods became reliable enough for large recordings.
ocar.challenge: Existing inference still needed refinement before trustworthy application to real data.
ocar.action: Dunn and Koo improve a deep residual convolutional method that integrates architecture advances with model-free partial correlation coefficients, and they assay it on synthetic ChaLearn Connectomics data.
ocar.resolution: The method outperforms published competition entries and can exceed 90% precision at 1% recall on validation sets. The authors suggest future application to larval zebrafish whole-brain imaging could recover on the order of 10^6 synaptic connections at a 10% false-discovery rate. The model generalizes across connection probabilities and should scale across GPUs.
ocar.future_work: They present the approach as a statistical complement to experiments and circuit hypotheses, with zebrafish in vivo imaging as a prospective target.

summaries.beginner: One way to guess who is connected to whom is to watch many cells fire and let a computer infer the links. This paper improves that kind of computer method on practice data and discusses using it on whole-brain activity movies from young zebrafish.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv in 2017, Dunn and Koo report gains on ChaLearn Connectomics synthetic benchmarks using residual convolutional networks plus partial correlations. They cite over 90% precision at 1% recall on validation data and outperform published competition methods. A prospective calculation for larval zebrafish imaging is on the order of a million connections at 10% false-discovery rate; that application is not performed here.
summaries.advanced: Results are on synthetic competition data. The 10^6 connections / 10% FDR figure is a suggestion for future in vivo zebrafish imaging, not an empirical recovery. Catalog tags list DS15 zebrafish and electron microscopy, but the abstract’s method is functional inference, not EM segmentation. Precision/recall is at a specific operating point (1% recall).

plain_language_summary: One way to guess who is connected to whom is to watch many cells fire and let a computer infer the links. This paper improves that kind of computer method on practice data and discusses using it on whole-brain activity movies from young zebrafish.

ocar.opportunity: Spinally projecting neurons in rat rostral ventrolateral medulla generate vasomotor sympathetic tone and are thought to receive convergent input from every neuraxis level; mapping that diffuse connectome would identify who actually drives them.
ocar.challenge: Factors determining their ongoing activity remain unresolved, and conventional mapping struggles with spatially scattered inputs.
ocar.action: Dempsey, McMullan and colleagues use a genetically restricted rabies strategy to label monosynaptic inputs to bulbospinal RVLM neurons, then map cells into an MRI volumetric atlas with a photomicrograph-to-coordinate alignment tool.
ocar.resolution: Most inputs (88–94%) lie in the brainstem, including putative respiratory neurons in pre-Bötzinger and post-inspiratory complexes likely to underlie respiratory-sympathetic coupling, plus a previously unrecognized input ventral to nucleus prepositus hypoglossi. Suprapontine inputs are sparse; cortex and amygdala contributions are almost absent.
ocar.future_work: The atlas workflow is offered as a platform to quantify, share, and independently reanalyze complete neuroanatomical datasets.

summaries.beginner: Some brainstem cells keep blood-vessel nerve activity going and were thought to hear from almost the whole brain. This rat study traces their direct inputs and finds most come from other brainstem cells, including breathing-related ones.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neural Circuits in 2017, Dempsey and colleagues map monosynaptic inputs to bulbospinal RVLM sympathetic premotor neurons in rat with recombinant rabies and an MRI-based volumetric atlas. They report 88–94% of inputs in the brainstem, including pre-Bötzinger and post-inspiratory candidates, a novel input ventral to prepositus hypoglossi, and almost no direct cortex or amygdala input. The alignment tool translates photomicrographs into Cartesian coordinates.
summaries.advanced: This is a viral-tracing mesoscale connectome, not EM. Rabies labels monosynaptic inputs to infected bulbospinal RVLM neurons; coverage depends on infection completeness. Percentages 88–94% are stated for brainstem share. Catalog organism is ‘other’ (rat).

plain_language_summary: Some brainstem cells keep blood-vessel nerve activity going and were thought to hear from almost the whole brain. This rat study traces their direct inputs and finds most come from other brainstem cells, including breathing-related ones.

ocar.opportunity: At the centenary of D’Arcy Thompson’s On Growth and Form, experimental advances make it possible to study how anatomical brain networks change in development and evolution.
ocar.challenge: Principles linking spatial and temporal factors to connectome development in health and disease, and thus to personalized treatment, are still being outlined.
ocar.action: Kaiser reviews recent results on how space and time shape connectome development and argues for the data types needed to connect development, structure, and function.
ocar.resolution: The review emphasizes that longitudinal studies, experimentally derived parameters for connection formation, and biologically realistic computational models are required.
ocar.future_work: Understanding developmental origins of brain diseases in individuals is presented as crucial for personalized treatment options.

summaries.beginner: Brains are not wired all at once; their connection patterns grow and change. This review discusses rules of that growth and why following them over time could help explain some brain disorders.
summaries.intermediate: In Trends in Cognitive Sciences in 2017, Marcus Kaiser outlines potential principles of connectome development, tying spatial and temporal factors to network change in health and disease. He argues that longitudinal measurements, experimentally derived connection-formation parameters, and biologically realistic models are needed to link development to structure and function. The article is a perspective, not a new dataset, and personalized-treatment implications are argued rather than demonstrated.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective/review, not a new dataset. Personalized-treatment implications are argued, not demonstrated. Catalog stage is modeling.

plain_language_summary: Brains are not wired all at once; their connection patterns grow and change. This review discusses rules of that growth and why following them over time could help explain some brain disorders.

ocar.opportunity: Function depends on both connectivity and biophysics; a real-time interface that shows structure and dynamics together would let users probe circuits by stimulation and ablation.
ocar.challenge: Supervised empirical search for functional stimulations is slow, and brute-force computational sweeps produce more data than insight.
ocar.action: Kim, Leahy and Shlizerman build Neural Interactome, a cross-platform graph visualization plus neural-dynamics simulator, implemented on a C. elegans nervous-system model with full connectome and dynamics, including ablation, zoom, review, and preset recording.
ocar.resolution: They show that stimulation and ablation help identify neurons shaping locomotion-related patterns, revisit experimental touch-response scenarios within seconds, and explore untested scenarios. The framework is designed to be generic to other networks.
ocar.future_work: Flexibility for other connectivity and dynamic models is presented as a generic methodology for neurobiological systems.

summaries.beginner: It is one thing to have a wiring diagram and another to poke the network and watch what happens. This software lets you stimulate or remove cells in a digital worm brain and see activity on the graph in real time.
summaries.intermediate: Published with a 2017 bioRxiv record and a Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience venue in the catalog, Kim, Leahy and Shlizerman introduce Neural Interactome: graph visualization combined with simulated or recorded multi-neuron time series, stimulation, and ablation. Using a C. elegans model they recover known touch-response patterns quickly and generate hypotheses for untested stimulations. Features include single-neuron zoom, temporal review, and presets.
summaries.advanced: Dynamics come from a model (or imported recordings), so conclusions about untested scenarios are hypotheses. Catalog journal field is bioRxiv while the DOI points at Frontiers; treat venue as the computational-neuroscience platform paper. Catalog dataset is DS01 C. elegans.

plain_language_summary: It is one thing to have a wiring diagram and another to poke the network and watch what happens. This software lets you stimulate or remove cells in a digital worm brain and see activity on the graph in real time.

ocar.opportunity: Larval Drosophila odor-taste learning is simple enough to be tractable yet rich enough for neurogenetics, psychology, and translational work, especially as a synaptic connectome and cell-specific transgenes become available.
ocar.challenge: Newcomers and classroom settings needed a detailed, multilingual, hands-on protocol rather than scattered methods notes.
ocar.action: Michels, Gerber and colleagues provide an illustrated manual for Pavlovian odor-reward learning in maggots, with scoring sheets, analysis guidance, and versions in English, German, French, Japanese, Spanish, and Italian.
ocar.resolution: They argue the paradigm is cheap, robust, already adopted by multiple labs, and suitable for earlier science education and a broader research community.
ocar.future_work: The manual is meant to lower the barrier to combining behavior with upcoming total synaptic connectome resources.

summaries.beginner: Young fruit flies can learn that a smell predicts a tasty reward, and the experiment is simple enough for teaching labs. This paper is a step-by-step, multi-language cookbook for running that learning test.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience in 2017, Michels, Gerber and colleagues publish a multilingual hands-on manual for larval Drosophila odor-reward Pavlovian conditioning. They emphasize low cost, robustness, classroom use, and alignment with forthcoming connectome and single-cell genetic tools. Supporting materials include scoring and display sheets.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods/teaching manual, not a circuit paper. Catalog dataset is DS03 Drosophila larva. Connectome utility is prospective in the abstract. Robustness claims are qualitative.

plain_language_summary: Young fruit flies can learn that a smell predicts a tasty reward, and the experiment is simple enough for teaching labs. This paper is a step-by-step, multi-language cookbook for running that learning test.

ocar.opportunity: Volume-EM connectomes plus simulators such as NEURON or GENESIS could, with channel and synapse models, simulate real circuits. Drosophila motion detection is a well-studied test case.
ocar.challenge: Geometry is available but synaptic models are not; it is also unclear how much physical detail simulations need.
ocar.action: Gornet and Scheffer insert approximate synapses matching known and estimated function, reproduce T4 direction selectivity, then compare models from fully detailed morphologies down to single-node neurons.
ocar.resolution: They verify extraction-plus-simulation functionality and find that much simpler, lumped models can be adequate for medulla neurons, reproducing the main motion-detector operation and confirming Gruntman’s result that dendritic computation is not required for this function. Reduced models are smaller and faster.
ocar.future_work: Adequacy of reduced models is stated for this medulla case; other computations may still need full morphology.

summaries.beginner: Once every cell’s shape is known, computers can try to replay the circuit, but that is slow if every tiny branch is included. This study of fly motion-detecting cells finds that much simpler stand-in cells can still produce the key computation.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv in 2017, Gornet and Scheffer combine extracted Drosophila motion-circuit geometry with approximate synapses in standard compartmental simulators. After reproducing T4 direction selectivity, they coarsen physical detail down to single-node neurons and still capture the main detector operation, in line with Gruntman that dendrites are not required for this function. Resource use drops with simpler models.
summaries.advanced: Synapses are approximate, not measured conductances. Results are for medulla motion detection, not a general theorem of reduction. Catalog organism is fly; no registry dataset is listed. Confirmation of Gruntman is computational, not a new physiology experiment.

plain_language_summary: Once every cell’s shape is known, computers can try to replay the circuit, but that is slow if every tiny branch is included. This study of fly motion-detecting cells finds that much simpler stand-in cells can still produce the key computation.

ocar.opportunity: Random dot product graphs are tractable yet can approximate graphs from stochastic block models to latent-position networks, offering a unified statistical framework for connectomes and social networks.
ocar.challenge: Graph inference needs analogues of classical Euclidean results—consistency, asymptotic normality, hypothesis tests—centered on spectral embeddings.
ocar.action: Athreya, Priebe, Vogelstein and colleagues survey spectral embeddings of adjacency and Laplacian matrices, single- and multi-sample tests, and applications including community detection and exploratory analysis of the Drosophila connectome.
ocar.resolution: They summarize consistency and asymptotic normality results for those embeddings, their use in hypothesis testing, and open problems in spectral graph inference.
ocar.future_work: The survey explicitly outlines current open problems in the spectral-inference program.

summaries.beginner: Many networks, including fly brain maps, can be treated as clouds of points whose overlap explains who is connected. This survey explains the statistics of that idea and how to test whether two networks differ.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Machine Learning Research in 2017, Athreya and colleagues review inference on random dot product graphs via adjacency and Laplacian spectral embeddings. They cover consistency, asymptotic normality, and hypothesis tests, with applications to social networks and exploratory analysis of the Drosophila connectome. The paper is a survey of a statistical paradigm, not a new reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: Catalog stages list preparation and graph analysis and organism fly; the Drosophila connectome is an application example, not a methods EM paper. Results cited are asymptotic and model-based; real connectomes may violate independent-edge assumptions.

plain_language_summary: Many networks, including fly brain maps, can be treated as clouds of points whose overlap explains who is connected. This survey explains the statistics of that idea and how to test whether two networks differ.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics aims to map brain connections at macroscopic, mesoscopic, and microscopic scales, and rich-club architecture is a prominent organizational idea at those scales.
ocar.challenge: How new findings refine the rich-club picture, and what remains unresolved across scales, needs journal-club synthesis.
ocar.action: Pedersen and Omidvarnia comment on further insight into the brain’s rich-club architecture, framing connectomics’ multi-scale aims after Bullmore and colleagues.
ocar.resolution: The available abstract introduces connectomics’ scales and situates rich-club discussion; it is a Journal of Neuroscience journal-club style piece rather than a primary mapping study.
ocar.future_work: Deeper empirical tests of rich-club function across scales remain the field’s task; this article is commentary.

summaries.beginner: Brains can be mapped as networks with a ‘rich club’ of highly connected hubs. This short commentary discusses newer insight into that idea.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neuroscience in 2016, Pedersen and Omidvarnia offer further commentary on rich-club architecture in connectomics, noting analyses from whole-brain to single-neuron scales. The piece is a journal-club perspective citing Bullmore, not a new dataset. Catalog axis is bridge.
summaries.advanced: The source abstract is truncated; claims beyond the multi-scale framing and rich-club topic are not supported here. No organism, dataset, or method tags are provided. Do not infer quantitative rich-club metrics.

plain_language_summary: Brains can be mapped as networks with a ‘rich club’ of highly connected hubs. This short commentary discusses newer insight into that idea.

ocar.opportunity: Multimodal 3-D imaging of cells and organelles is more accessible, so high-performance segmentation and analysis tools are needed to remove a workflow bottleneck.
ocar.challenge: Large multidimensional light- and electron-microscopy datasets were hard to process, visualize, and quantify in one open environment.
ocar.action: Belevich, Jokitalo and colleagues present Microscopy Image Browser, an open-source package with plug-in extensibility, tutorials, and examples on light and electron microscopy.
ocar.resolution: They provide a freely available platform intended to improve quantitative use of acquired volumetric data, with user-customizable plug-ins.
ocar.future_work: Open-source plug-ins are invited so labs can tailor the program to specific imaging needs.

summaries.beginner: Modern microscopes produce huge 3D pictures that are hard to measure. This paper introduces free software to outline and analyze those pictures of cells.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Biology in 2016, Belevich, Jokitalo and colleagues release Microscopy Image Browser for high-performance segmentation and processing of multidimensional datasets. The open-source environment supports plug-ins and is demonstrated on light and electron microscopy, with tutorials for rapid uptake. It is software infrastructure rather than a biological result, and the abstract does not report numeric segmentation benchmarks.
summaries.advanced: This is software infrastructure, not a biological result. Catalog method is electron microscopy among intended data types. No quantitative benchmark scores appear in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Modern microscopes produce huge 3D pictures that are hard to measure. This paper introduces free software to outline and analyze those pictures of cells.

ocar.opportunity: High-resolution anatomical and functional connectomes now exist, but the molecular mechanisms that set precise connectivity and synaptic properties remain harder to map—a molecular synaptic connectome underlying the neural connectome.
ocar.challenge: Genetic approaches to synaptic connectivity and function have power and limitations; linking them to proteomic methods is still difficult.
ocar.action: Schreiner, de Wit and colleagues review genetic analyses of synaptic connectivity and discuss how proteomic developments might elucidate the molecular synaptic connectome.
ocar.resolution: They describe strengths and limits of genetics and point to proteomics as a path toward the molecular layer of circuit maps.
ocar.future_work: Methodological development in proteomics is presented as the route to that molecular connectome.

summaries.beginner: Knowing which cells touch is not the same as knowing which molecules make those contacts specific and strong. This opinion piece discusses how genetics and protein surveys might fill that gap.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology in 2016, Schreiner, Savas, Herzog, Brose and de Wit review synapse biology in a circuit-age setting. They contrast the resolution of emerging anatomical and functional connectomes with the difficulty of assigning molecular mechanisms to connectivity and transmission. Proteomic methods are discussed as a path toward a molecular synaptic connectome underlying neural wiring diagrams.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a methods benchmark. Catalog axis is biological_application. No new numbers or datasets are given.

plain_language_summary: Knowing which cells touch is not the same as knowing which molecules make those contacts specific and strong. This opinion piece discusses how genetics and protein surveys might fill that gap.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics and other neuroanatomy need brain-banking methods that combine long-term ice-free storage with excellent ultrastructural resolution and that scale by perfusion to large brains.
ocar.challenge: Conventional banking can degrade ultrastructure over time or fail to scale; vitrification of whole brains after fixation is nontrivial.
ocar.action: McIntyre and Fahy perfuse-fix rabbit and pig brains with a glutaraldehyde-based fixative, slowly raise ethylene glycol to 65% w/v, vitrify at −135 °C, rewarm, remove cryoprotectant by perfusion or diffusion, and evaluate by electron microscopy and FIB-SEM.
ocar.resolution: Preservation is described as uniformly excellent, with traceable processes and crisp synapses in both species. ASC yields a perfusable aldehyde-preserved brain after cryoprotectant removal.
ocar.future_work: The method is presented as enabling assays on stored brains of any size because chemicals are delivered by perfusion.

summaries.beginner: To study a brain’s tiny wiring later, you need a way to store it without ice crystals wrecking the structure. This paper shows a chemical-then-deep-freeze method for rabbit and pig brains that keeps synapses looking sharp.
summaries.intermediate: In Cryobiology in 2015, McIntyre and Fahy introduce aldehyde-stabilized cryopreservation: glutaraldehyde fixation, stepwise ethylene glycol to 65% w/v, vitrification at −135 °C, then rewarming and cryoprotectant removal. Electron microscopy and FIB-SEM of rabbit and pig brains show traceable processes and crisp synapses. Perfusion delivery is argued to scale to large brains.
summaries.advanced: ‘Uniformly excellent’ is the authors’ qualitative EM assessment. Species are rabbit and pig, not mouse or fly connectome volumes. Catalog method includes FIB-SEM for evaluation. Functional viability is not claimed; the product is an aldehyde-preserved, optionally re-perfused anatomical specimen.

plain_language_summary: To study a brain’s tiny wiring later, you need a way to store it without ice crystals wrecking the structure. This paper shows a chemical-then-deep-freeze method for rabbit and pig brains that keeps synapses looking sharp.

ocar.opportunity: Electron-microscopy connectomes can identify the exact neurons and synapses that compute visual motion, a classic problem whose mechanism was frustrated by incomplete wiring knowledge.
ocar.challenge: Light microscopy infers connections from arbor overlap; that is not the same as counted synapses, and motion circuitry needed comprehensive EM reconstruction.
ocar.action: Takemura reviews recent EM connectomics of Drosophila visual circuitry that identified the concrete neuronal circuit computing motion signals.
ocar.resolution: Comprehensiveness of EM reconstruction, with precise synaptic counts rather than overlap estimates, enabled identification of the motion-computation circuit. The review highlights how connectomes ground neuronal function in identified wiring.
ocar.future_work: The piece presents fly visual connectomics as a foundation for further mechanistic work on computation.

summaries.beginner: How a fly sees motion was a famous puzzle because the exact wiring was missing. This review explains how electron-microscope maps of the fly’s visual system finally named the cells and synapses that do that job.
summaries.intermediate: In Microscopy in 2015, Shin-ya Takemura reviews EM connectomics of the fruit fly visual system, emphasizing motion detection. Compared with light-microscopic overlap estimates, EM provides unequivocal connections and synaptic counts, which enabled identification of the motion-computing circuit. The paper is a review of recent reconstruction work rather than a new volume.
summaries.advanced: This is a review; circuit identification is attributed to recent connectomic studies, not a single new dataset here. Catalog organism is fly and method electron microscopy.

plain_language_summary: How a fly sees motion was a famous puzzle because the exact wiring was missing. This review explains how electron-microscope maps of the fly’s visual system finally named the cells and synapses that do that job.

ocar.opportunity: A binding code among Drosophila immunoglobulin superfamily proteins could explain how specific synaptic partnerships form in neuromuscular and visual systems.
ocar.challenge: Which cell-surface interactions actually control terminal placement, trophic responses, transmission, and target survival was unclear.
ocar.action: Carrillo, Zinn, Garcia and colleagues define a Dpr–DIP interaction network (21 Dprs binding 9 DIPs), solve structural complementarity of the binding code, and examine six genes in larval and pupal neurons, neuromuscular terminals, and the visual system.
ocar.resolution: Each examined gene is expressed in a unique neuronal subset. Dpr11–DIP-γ interactions affect presynaptic development, trophic responses, and neurotransmission. In the visual system, dpr11 is selective for Rh4-using yR7s whose Dm8 targets express DIP-γ; mutants send yR7 terminals beyond layer M6, and DIP-γ is required for Dm8 survival or differentiation.
ocar.future_work: The findings suggest Dpr–DIP interactions are important synaptic-connectivity determinants, inviting tests of the remaining family members.

summaries.beginner: Nerve cells use surface proteins as nametags to choose partners. This fly paper maps a family of matching nametags and shows that breaking one pair scrambles connections in muscles and in the eye.
summaries.intermediate: In Cell in 2015, Carrillo, Özkan, Zinn, Garcia and colleagues describe a 21-by-9 Dpr–DIP immunoglobulin-superfamily binding network whose specificity appears to reflect shape complementarity. Functional work on Dpr11 and DIP-γ shows neuromuscular and yR7–Dm8 visual phenotypes, including overshoot of yR7 terminals past medulla layer M6 and loss of DIP-γ-dependent Dm8 survival or differentiation. Six examined dpr/DIP genes each label unique neuronal subsets.
summaries.advanced: Only 6 of 30 family genes are examined functionally here. Visual phenotypes are genetic, not an EM-proofread circuit. Shape complementarity is presented as the structural basis of the code. Catalog organism is fly.

plain_language_summary: Nerve cells use surface proteins as nametags to choose partners. This fly paper maps a family of matching nametags and shows that breaking one pair scrambles connections in muscles and in the eye.

ocar.opportunity: Circuit mapping still bottlenecks on reconstructing and editing neuronal morphologies from fluorescence images, despite automatic algorithms.
ocar.challenge: Existing tools lacked a combination of comprehensive editing, seed-based tracing plus path search, and parallel 2D/3D visualization in a WYSIWYG workflow centered on the SWC standard.
ocar.action: Feng, Zhao and Kim implement neuTube 1.0 as open-source software designed around SWC, with parallel 2D/3D views and tracing/editing that also edits reconstructions from other tools.
ocar.resolution: They compare neuTube 1.0 to Neuromantic and Neurostudio and argue it allows efficient reconstruction from fluorescence data. Software, documentation, and video tutorials are hosted at a public site.
ocar.future_work: The design is intended to support sharing via archives such as NeuroMorpho.org through standard SWC files.

summaries.beginner: Turning microscope pictures of neurons into stick-figure tracings is still slow. This paper introduces free software that lets you trace and fix those shapes in linked 2D and 3D views.
summaries.intermediate: In eNeuro in 2015, Feng, Zhao and Kim present neuTube 1.0, an SWC-centered open-source reconstructor with parallel 2D/3D visualization, seed-based tracing, path searching, and extensive editing. They compare it with Neuromantic and Neurostudio for fluorescence-image reconstruction. Files remain compatible with other SWC tools and archives.
summaries.advanced: Comparisons are qualitative in the abstract. The software targets fluorescence morphology, not EM segmentation. Catalog stage is proofreading.

plain_language_summary: Turning microscope pictures of neurons into stick-figure tracings is still slow. This paper introduces free software that lets you trace and fix those shapes in linked 2D and 3D views.

ocar.opportunity: Serial ultrastructural observation with scanning electron microscopy, plus tissue preparation that increases heavy-metal contrast, makes complete neuronal connection maps—connectomes—more tractable than classical serial-section TEM alone.
ocar.challenge: Methods differ in resolution, speed, re-observation, and target volume, and huge datasets still require automated segmentation and 3D reconstruction.
ocar.action: Ohno and colleagues review SEM-based volume imaging approaches toward connectomics, comparing advantages and disadvantages across observation conditions.
ocar.resolution: They argue method choice should depend on tissue size, required resolution, and need for re-observation, and that automation of segmentation and reconstruction is critical for larger brain volumes.
ocar.future_work: Future improvements in acquisition and analysis are awaited to relate whole connectomes to consciousness, intelligence, and memory as structural bases—an aspirational framing in the review.

summaries.beginner: Mapping every connection in a piece of brain needs 3D electron-microscope pictures. This review compares newer scanning-electron methods for stacking those pictures and notes that computers must help outline the cells.
summaries.intermediate: In Microscopy in 2015, Ohno, Katoh and colleagues review three-dimensional volume imaging with electron microscopy toward connectomics. They contrast SEM-based serial imaging and heavy-metal preparation with conventional serial-section TEM, stressing tradeoffs in resolution, speed, and re-observation. Dataset scale is identified as a remaining obstacle requiring automated segmentation.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods review, not a new volume. Links to consciousness and memory are prospective, not empirical results. Catalog method is serial-section EM; stages include sectioning, acquisition, and segmentation.

plain_language_summary: Mapping every connection in a piece of brain needs 3D electron-microscope pictures. This review compares newer scanning-electron methods for stacking those pictures and notes that computers must help outline the cells.

ocar.opportunity: As reconstructed connectomes grow beyond hundreds of neurons, clustering similarly shaped neurons would help find motifs and types. Skeleton representations of 3D shape are a practical input.
ocar.challenge: Reasoning about large maps is limited without automatic grouping of morphologically similar cells.
ocar.action: Zhao and Plaza introduce location-sensitive clustering algorithms for neuronal skeletons and apply them to neurons reconstructed from the Drosophila medulla.
ocar.resolution: They report high-accuracy clustering on medulla reconstructions. The algorithms are intended to aid connectome analysis by grouping similarly shaped neurons.
ocar.future_work: The methods are offered for increasingly large (or partial) connectomes as reconstruction scales up.

summaries.beginner: Once many neurons have been traced, it helps to group the ones that look alike. This paper describes computer methods that cluster fly visual neurons by the shape and location of their branches.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2014 arXiv paper, Zhao and Plaza propose location-sensitive clustering of skeletonized 3D neurons and show results on reconstructions from the Drosophila medulla, reporting high accuracy. The goal is to support type assignment and motif analysis as connectomes grow past the scale of C. elegans. The abstract does not give a numeric accuracy score, and the clustering is morphological rather than a new EM segmentation method.
summaries.advanced: ‘High-accuracy’ is not given as a numeric score in the abstract. Catalog dataset/organism fields list DS01 C. elegans, but the title and abstract analyze Drosophila medulla reconstructions—ground types in the abstract. Method tag ‘Network motifs’ is catalog metadata, not an EM modality.

plain_language_summary: Once many neurons have been traced, it helps to group the ones that look alike. This paper describes computer methods that cluster fly visual neurons by the shape and location of their branches.

ocar.opportunity: Neural systems show modular, often hierarchical organization across species; relating hierarchy to processing, including where a ‘top’ sits for functions such as consciousness, is a central challenge.
ocar.challenge: Nodes are often treated as uniform despite differences in inhibition versus excitation, morphology, and gene expression, which complicates structure–function–dynamics links.
ocar.action: Kaiser discusses common connectome constraints from C. elegans and Drosophila to humans, including effects of topology on synchrony, oscillation, and activity propagation reported in earlier studies.
ocar.resolution: The preprint frames hierarchy, modularity, and node heterogeneity as shared constraints and open questions rather than presenting a new reconstruction.
ocar.future_work: Understanding how hierarchical organization maps onto processing remains a main challenge of the field as stated here.

summaries.beginner: Worm, fly, and human brains all seem to be built from modules stacked in layers. This short paper discusses those shared wiring constraints and why treating every cell as identical is too simple.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2014 arXiv preprint, Marcus Kaiser reviews common connectome constraints from C. elegans and Drosophila to Homo sapiens. He emphasizes modular and hierarchical organization, topology’s influence on dynamics, and the problem of locating a processing top.
