They note productive non-expert contributions to tasks such as organelle segmentation in volume EM and offer methodological principles from multiple teams. Catalog axis is training/outreach.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods/community synthesis, not a new segmentation algorithm. Catalog methods include volume EM; stages include segmentation, proofreading, infrastructure, and acquisition. Quantitative accuracy of citizen labels is referenced as demonstrated in recent research, not re-measured here.

plain_language_summary: Some 3D cell pictures are so large that scientists invite the public to help outline them online. This article gathers lessons from projects that used the Zooniverse website for that kind of biology.

ocar.opportunity: Sleep both prepares the brain to learn and consolidates new memories; Drosophila genetics, a mapped connectome, and known sleep and memory mechanisms make the fly a model for that interaction.
ocar.challenge: Molecular and network mechanisms of sleep-dependent versus sleep-independent consolidation, and of learning-induced sleep drive, remain incomplete despite clear behavioral facts.
ocar.action: Marquand, Boto and colleagues review how sleep affects acquisition and consolidation in Drosophila, including deprivation effects and recent circuit work on sleep-dependent consolidation and a neural switch between strategies.
ocar.resolution: The review states that sleep facilitates learning in wild-type and memory-impaired animals, deprivation impairs acquisition, sleep is paramount for consolidation, and learning can promote sleep drive. Recent studies described substrates of sleep-dependent consolidation and the switch between sleep-dependent and sleep-independent strategies.
ocar.future_work: Questions still awaiting investigation are explicitly flagged as the review’s horizon.

summaries.beginner: Sleep helps animals learn and store memories, and fruit flies show the same benefit. This review summarizes how fly sleep and memory interact and what circuit findings have recently emerged.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Physiology in 2023, Marquand, Roselli, Cervantes-Sandoval and Boto review sleep’s roles across memory stages in Drosophila. They summarize that sleep aids learning even in memory-impaired flies, deprivation blocks acquisition, consolidation depends on sleep, and learning itself can increase sleep drive. Recent work on sleep-dependent consolidation circuits and a switch versus sleep-independent strategies is highlighted.
summaries.advanced: This is a review. Catalog organism is fly; stages include acquisition and infrastructure. ‘Paramount’ consolidation is the authors’ synthesis, not a new experiment. Remaining mechanistic gaps are acknowledged.

plain_language_summary: Sleep helps animals learn and store memories, and fruit flies show the same benefit. This review summarizes how fly sleep and memory interact and what circuit findings have recently emerged.

ocar.opportunity: Cortical and subcortical tissue removed during tumor and epilepsy surgery is often discarded yet can support human clinical and basic research if handled as viable access tissue.
ocar.challenge: Operating-room handling must be standardized for electrophysiology, electron microscopy, and organotypic cultures without compromising patient safety.
ocar.action: Straehle, Schnell and colleagues refine surgical microdissection principles over 36 experimental rounds: rapid preparation under one minute, preserved cortical axis, minimal trauma, pointed scalpel, no cauterization or blunt dissection, constant irrigation, and retrieval without forceps or suction, with immediate immersion in carbogenated NMDG-aCSF or hibernation medium.
ocar.resolution: After a single introduction, multiple surgeons obtained samples at least 5 mm spanning all cortical layers and white matter. Small 5–7 mm samples were ideal for acute slices and electrophysiology. No adverse events from sample resection were observed.
ocar.future_work: The standardized extraction is presented as a foundation for human-to-human translational research on living brain tissue.

summaries.beginner: Bits of human brain removed during necessary surgery can be used for research instead of being thrown away, if they are cut out gently and quickly. This surgical report lists practical rules that kept samples healthy and caused no extra harm to patients.
summaries.intermediate: In Acta Neurochirurgica in 2023, Straehle and colleagues describe microdissection of human cortical access tissue across 36 experimental rounds. Seven operating-room principles yielded ≥5 mm full-thickness samples; 5–7 mm pieces suited acute electrophysiology. Tissue went immediately into cold carbogenated NMDG-aCSF or hibernation medium for physiology, EM, or organotypic culture. No adverse events were observed.
summaries.advanced: Safety is reported as no adverse events in this series, not a randomized trial. Minimum dimension 5 mm and ideal 5–7 mm are as stated. Catalog method includes electron microscopy among downstream uses; axis is health_translation. ‘n = 36’ is rounds of experimental refinement.

plain_language_summary: Bits of human brain removed during necessary surgery can be used for research instead of being thrown away, if they are cut out gently and quickly. This surgical report lists practical rules that kept samples healthy and caused no extra harm to patients.

ocar.opportunity: A multimodal larval zebrafish brain atlas that co-visualizes gene expression, single-neuron tracings, transgenes, and activity would accelerate in silico queries of cell types and circuits.
ocar.challenge: Registering multiplexed expression and immediate-early-gene activity into an existing morphological atlas at single-cell resolution is nontrivial.
ocar.action: Shainer, Baier, Kunst and colleagues map 200 marker genes by multiplexed HCR, register them to the Max Planck Zebrafish Brain (mapzebrain) atlas, and add cfos activity maps from freely swimming larvae.
ocar.resolution: As proof of concept they identify a novel cerebellar eurydendroid class that expresses calb2a, projects to hypothalamus, and is activated after food ingestion. The resource links molecular identity to tracings, transgenes, anatomy, and behavior-related activity.
ocar.future_work: The atlas is intended for rapid marker identification and for bridging molecular and circuit levels.

summaries.beginner: This atlas paints where 200 genes are turned on in a young zebrafish brain and lines those maps up with known cell shapes and with which cells were recently active. Using it, the authors found a new cerebellar cell type that lights up after the fish eats.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv in 2022, Shainer, Kuehn, Laurell, Kunst, Baier and colleagues add multiplexed HCR maps of 200 marker genes and cfos activity to the mapzebrain larval zebrafish atlas. Registration enables co-visualization with single-neuron tracings, transgenes, and parcellations. They describe calb2a-positive eurydendroid cells projecting to hypothalamus and activated after food ingestion.
summaries.advanced: The initial marker set is 200 genes. Activity is cfos in freely swimming larvae, not a full functional connectome. Catalog dataset is DS15 zebrafish; stages include segmentation and proofreading. ‘Novel class’ is defined by the combined molecular, projection, and activity criteria stated.

plain_language_summary: This atlas paints where 200 genes are turned on in a young zebrafish brain and lines those maps up with known cell shapes and with which cells were recently active. Using it, the authors found a new cerebellar cell type that lights up after the fish eats.

ocar.opportunity: Public archives for atomic models (PDB) and cryo-EM reconstructions (EMDB) left a community need to store raw cryo-EM images plus volume EM and X-ray tomography reconstructions for validation, software development, and training.
ocar.challenge: Growth now exceeds a thousand entries and two petabytes, stressing deposition, search, visualization, download, and reuse.
ocar.action: Iudin, Patwardhan and colleagues describe EMPIAR’s deposition system, entry pages, search/visualize/download tools, and REST API.
ocar.resolution: EMPIAR archives raw cryo-EM and 3D reconstructions from volume EM and X-ray tomography, with over a thousand entries totalling over 2 petabytes.
ocar.future_work: Fast data growth and enhancing reusability are named as significant future challenges.

summaries.beginner: Scientists need a public attic for the huge raw pictures behind electron-microscope structures, not only the final 3D maps. EMPIAR is that attic, now holding over two petabytes of data.
summaries.intermediate: In Nucleic Acids Research (catalog journal field bioRxiv; DOI 10.1093/nar/gkac1062) in 2022, Iudin, Korir, Kleywegt, Patwardhan and colleagues present EMPIAR as the public archive for raw cryo-EM images and for volume EM and X-ray tomography reconstructions. Resources include deposition, search, visualization, download, and a REST API. Scale is over 1,000 entries and over 2 petabytes.
summaries.advanced: Catalog journal lists bioRxiv while the DOI is NAR; treat as the NAR archive paper. Challenges of growth and reusability are acknowledged. Catalog methods include X-ray microscopy and volume EM. This is infrastructure, not a biological result.

plain_language_summary: Scientists need a public attic for the huge raw pictures behind electron-microscope structures, not only the final 3D maps. EMPIAR is that attic, now holding over two petabytes of data.

ocar.opportunity: Whether a fruit-fly connectome’s topology can improve machine-learning reservoirs is a concrete test of connectome-derived constraints on computation.
ocar.challenge: Classical echo-state networks use a fixed random reservoir; replacing it with connectome topology may or may not help chaotic time-series prediction.
ocar.action: Morra and Daley replace the ESN reservoir with a female fruit-fly connectome-derived connectivity matrix (FFESN) and compare validation mean-squared error to random ESNs across four train-size and split settings.
ocar.resolution: In all four trial sets the FFESN either significantly outperforms and has lower variance than the ESN, or simply has lower variance.
ocar.future_work: The result is specific to this prediction task and one female fly connectome-derived matrix.

summaries.beginner: Some computer models use a large tangle of random connections as their working memory. This paper swaps in a fruit-fly wiring pattern instead and finds the fly-inspired tangle is at least more stable, and sometimes more accurate, on a forecasting task.
summaries.intermediate: At IJCNN in 2022, Morra and Daley impose fruit-fly connectome topology on an echo-state network for chaotic time-series prediction. Across four combinations of training input size and train–validate splits, the fly-derived reservoir either beats a random ESN on validation MSE with lower variance, or matches with lower variance. The connectome is from a particular female fly.
summaries.advanced: Performance is on a chaotic time-series task, not a neuroscience decoding task. ‘Significantly outperforms’ is as stated without a p-value in the abstract. Catalog organism is fly. Topology is a connectivity matrix derived from a connectome, not a biophysical simulation.

plain_language_summary: Some computer models use a large tangle of random connections as their working memory. This paper swaps in a fruit-fly wiring pattern instead and finds the fly-inspired tangle is at least more stable, and sometimes more accurate, on a forecasting task.

ocar.opportunity: Mouse V1 connectome statistics vary by cell type and dataset, making general rules for visual processing hard to see. A compact circuit model fitted to physiology could identify which weights matter.
ocar.challenge: High-dimensional, condition-variable anatomical data are difficult to relate to visual function; even within a type, statistics differ across datasets.
ocar.action: Toyoizumi comments on Kraynyukova et al., who fit a stabilized supralinear network of excitatory and inhibitory V1 populations receiving dLGN input—six weights plus a nonlinearity exponent—to in vivo responses to gratings of varying contrast and orientation.
ocar.resolution: The commentary frames SSN model-based analysis as addressing identification of important parameters, data variability, and linking anatomy to visual processing in mouse V1.
ocar.future_work: As a commentary, it points to the fitted SSN as a route to general rules rather than presenting a new experiment.

summaries.beginner: Maps of mouse visual cortex show messy, cell-type-specific connection strengths. This commentary discusses a modeling study that fits a simple excitatory–inhibitory circuit to real visual responses to find order in that mess.
summaries.intermediate: In PNAS in 2022, T. Toyoizumi discusses work by Kraynyukova et al. fitting a stabilized supralinear network (excitatory and inhibitory V1 populations, thalamic input, six weights, exponent n) to mouse dLGN and V1 responses to gratings of varying contrast and orientation. The commentary argues such models address parameter identification, dataset variability, and structure–function links in V1 connectome data.
summaries.advanced: The source abstract is truncated and is a commentary, not the primary SSN paper. Catalog dataset is DS01 C. elegans, which does not match this mouse V1 topic—ground science in the abstract (mouse V1/dLGN). Do not invent fit quality or weight values beyond the model’s listed six weights and exponent n.

plain_language_summary: Maps of mouse visual cortex show messy, cell-type-specific connection strengths. This commentary discusses a modeling study that fits a simple excitatory–inhibitory circuit to real visual responses to find order in that mess.

ocar.opportunity: The fruit-fly brain’s efficiency, robustness, and economy are thought to live in connectivity, but direct evidence was limited. Percolation controlled by synaptic excitation–inhibition balance could explain those properties as phase-transition byproducts.
ocar.challenge: Technical and theoretical gaps left origins of those advantageous properties unproven on a large fly connectome.
ocar.action: Tian and Sun study functional-connectivity formation as percolation on the largest available fruit-fly brain connectome while varying E/I balance.
ocar.resolution: Properties emerge when E/I reaches 3:7; an optimal simultaneous regime is E/I 1:1, consistent with prior in vitro predictions; above 3:2, anatomical connectivity limits further gains.
ocar.future_work: Percolation is proposed as a window on emergence of multiple brain properties, inviting tests on other connectomes.

summaries.beginner: Brains are efficient, sturdy, and cheap in how they send information, and people often credit the wiring. This fly-connectome study treats turning up excitation versus inhibition like a phase change, and finds those good properties appear together at particular balance points.
summaries.intermediate: In Network Neuroscience in 2022, Tian and Sun model functional connectivity as percolation on a large Drosophila brain connectome controlled by synaptic excitation-inhibition balance. Advantageous efficiency, robustness, and economy appear as transition byproducts at an E/I ratio of 3:7 and are jointly optimal near 1:1, matching prior in vitro predictions. Beyond 3:2, static anatomy limits further gains in those properties.
summaries.advanced: E/I ratios 3:7, 1:1, and 3:2 are model control points as stated. ‘Largest yet’ fly connectome is not named. Functional connectivity is generated by the percolation process, not measured in vivo. Catalog organism is fly.

plain_language_summary: Brains are efficient, sturdy, and cheap in how they send information, and people often credit the wiring. This fly-connectome study treats turning up excitation versus inhibition like a phase change, and finds those good properties appear together at particular balance points.

ocar.opportunity: Deep networks segment neurons in EM volumes well only when labels are plentiful; unlabeled volumes still contain usable structure.
ocar.challenge: If required manual annotations cannot be reached, supervised neuron segmentation becomes fragile.
ocar.action: Huang, Xiong and colleagues propose two-stage semi-supervised learning: pretrain by reconstructing original volumes from perturbed ones, then regularize supervised training with pixel-level consistency between unlabeled images and their perturbations.
ocar.resolution: On representative EM datasets they report up to 400% gain on the VOI metric with few labels, on par with a model trained on ten times more labeled data in a fully supervised manner. Code is released.
ocar.future_work: The method is aimed at EM volumes where labels remain scarce.

summaries.beginner: Teaching a computer to outline neurons usually needs many hand-drawn examples. This paper first has the network rebuild jumbled pictures, then checks that it gives the same outlines on slightly altered unlabeled pictures, stretching a few labels much further.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging in 2022, Huang, Chen, Xiong and colleagues introduce reinforced consistency learning for semi-supervised neuron segmentation in EM. Reconstruction pretraining plus unlabeled perturbation consistency yields up to 400% VOI improvement with few labels, comparable to supervised training with tenfold more labels. Code is available.
summaries.advanced: The 400% VOI gain is an upper value with very few labels as stated. Comparability to ten times the labels is as claimed for that setting. Catalog stages include segmentation, proofreading, and graph analysis. Datasets are ‘representative EM datasets,’ unnamed in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Teaching a computer to outline neurons usually needs many hand-drawn examples. This paper first has the network rebuild jumbled pictures, then checks that it gives the same outlines on slightly altered unlabeled pictures, stretching a few labels much further.

ocar.opportunity: The adult human brain has about 86 billion neurons; linking synaptic, cellular, and whole-organ scales is a central scientific goal. C. elegans already has a complete structural–functional model for 302 neurons, highlighting the gap.
ocar.challenge: Human connectome detail comparable to C. elegans is far off, and data growth raises processing and storage demands that strain supercomputing.
ocar.action: Amunts and Lippert discuss how unraveling human brain structure generates big-data challenges and may force creative computational solutions beyond neuroscience.
ocar.resolution: They argue that decoding the human connectome, signal transduction, and function is tied to exponentially growing computational and storage needs.
ocar.future_work: Solutions beyond current neuroscience workflows are presented as a likely outcome of those demands.

summaries.beginner: The human brain has tens of billions of nerve cells, and pictures of them at many zoom levels overflow even supercomputers. This Science piece explains why brain mapping is becoming a high-performance computing problem.
summaries.intermediate: In Science in 2021, Amunts and Lippert contrast the complete C. elegans connectome and structural-functional model of 302 neurons with the about 86 billion-neuron human brain. They argue that multi-scale human mapping creates exponential computational and storage challenges. Those demands may drive creative solutions beyond neuroscience itself; the article is a perspective, not a new reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective. The 86 billion figure is cited from (1) as stated. Catalog dataset is DS01 C. elegans as the comparison complete connectome. No new human reconstruction is reported.

plain_language_summary: The human brain has tens of billions of nerve cells, and pictures of them at many zoom levels overflow even supercomputers. This Science piece explains why brain mapping is becoming a high-performance computing problem.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-mouse-brain mapping with serial two-photon, fMOST, light-sheet, VISoR, or MRI requires registration to a standard atlas to characterize neuron types and wiring.
ocar.challenge: Cross-modal registration is hard because of anatomical variation and artifacts from sample preparation and imaging modality.
ocar.action: Peng, Zeng and colleagues introduce mBrainAligner, using coherent landmark mapping and deep networks to align whole mouse brains to the Allen Common Coordinate Framework, and they build an fMOST-based atlas for single-cell mapping.
ocar.resolution: They generate a whole-brain map of three-dimensional single-neuron morphology and neuron cell types using the method. mBrainAligner is presented as a cross-modal registration platform.
ocar.future_work: The fMOST atlas is intended to facilitate single-cell mapping in that modality going forward.

summaries.beginner: Different microscopes take whole-mouse-brain pictures that do not automatically sit in the same standard space. This paper’s software lines those pictures up to the Allen atlas so cell shapes can be compared.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods in 2021, Peng, Qu, Li, Wang, Gong, Hawrylycz, Zeng and colleagues present mBrainAligner for registering whole mouse brains from multiple 3D modalities to the Allen Common Coordinate Framework via coherent landmarks and deep networks. They also construct a fluorescence micro-optical sectioning tomography mouse brain atlas. Using the pipeline they generate a whole-brain map of three-dimensional single-neuron morphology and neuron cell types.
summaries.advanced: Modalities listed include serial two-photon, fMOST, light-sheet, VISoR, and MRI. Catalog methods include light-sheet, two-photon, and serial two-photon. Registration quality metrics are not in the abstract. This is alignment infrastructure plus an atlas product.

plain_language_summary: Different microscopes take whole-mouse-brain pictures that do not automatically sit in the same standard space. This paper’s software lines those pictures up to the Allen atlas so cell shapes can be compared.

ocar.opportunity: Dopamine neurons can cotransmit glutamate; functional roles of that cotransmission, from synapses to behavior, are only emerging and may matter for therapy.
ocar.challenge: How glutamate cotransmission from ventral midbrain dopamine neurons shapes synaptic signaling, development, and behavior needed a synthesis across species and methods, including connectome mapping.
ocar.action: Eskenazi, Rayport, Chuhma and colleagues review evidence from cultures through in vivo work, functional connectome mapping, and behavioral analyses of dopamine-neuron glutamate cotransmission.
ocar.resolution: Connectome mapping shows robust forebrain connections, notably onto cholinergic interneurons in nucleus accumbens medial shell and lateral dorsal striatum, while glutamate markers peak embryonically and rise after toxins, suggesting neuroprotection. Behaviorally, cotransmission contributes to psychostimulant responses, positive valence and cognition, with subtler negative-valence roles. Implications span addiction, schizophrenia, and Parkinson disease.
ocar.future_work: Therapeutic implications are discussed as informed by these circuit roles rather than as tested treatments.

summaries.beginner: Some dopamine cells also release glutamate, the brain’s main go signal. This review explains what that dual message does at connections, during development, and in behavior, with notes on addiction and Parkinson’s disease.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neural Circuits in 2021, Eskenazi, Malave, Mingote, Yetnikoff, Ztaou, Velicu, Rayport and Chuhma review glutamate cotransmission from ventral midbrain dopamine neurons. They highlight connectome targets (especially cholinergic interneurons in accumbens medial shell and lateral dorsal striatum), developmental and toxin-induced increases in glutamate markers, and behavioral roles in psychostimulant response and valence/cognition. Disease context includes addiction, schizophrenia, and Parkinson disease.
summaries.advanced: This is a review spanning cultures to behavior. Catalog axis is biological_application. Neuroprotective interpretation of marker increases is suggested, not proven. Therapeutic implications are inferential.

plain_language_summary: Some dopamine cells also release glutamate, the brain’s main go signal. This review explains what that dual message does at connections, during development, and in behavior, with notes on addiction and Parkinson’s disease.

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy, especially FIB-SEM in a resolution/speed ‘Goldilocks zone,’ can quantify virus–cell architectures in 3D at tens of nanometers or better over microns-thick samples.
ocar.challenge: Virologists need a practical primer on room-temperature FIB-SEM within the broader vEM landscape.
ocar.action: Baena, Narayan and colleagues provide a primer on FIB-SEM for viral infection studies and apply it to an in vitro SARS-CoV-2 infection model, quantifying viral densities and membrane curvature.
ocar.resolution: Accurate quantitation shows SARS-CoV-2 particles preferentially at plasma-membrane regions of positive mean curvature.
ocar.future_work: The primer is intended to enable similar architectural studies of other viral infections.

summaries.beginner: Some electron microscopes shave and photograph a sample over and over to build a 3D view of infected cells. This guide explains that method and shows that SARS-CoV-2 particles prefer curved patches of the cell surface.
summaries.intermediate: In Viruses in 2021, Baena, Conrad, Friday, Narayan and colleagues introduce FIB-SEM as a volume-EM approach for virus–cell architecture and apply it to in vitro SARS-CoV-2 infection. Automated mill-and-image cycles yield 3D views at tens of nanometers or less over microns-thick specimens. They report viruses preferentially at plasma-membrane areas with positive mean curvature.
summaries.advanced: The infection study is in vitro. Catalog dataset DS13 MICrONS and organism mouse do not match the SARS-CoV-2 in vitro primer—ground biology in the abstract. Curvature preference is for positive mean curvature as quantified. This is room-temperature FIB-SEM, not cryo-FIB.

plain_language_summary: Some electron microscopes shave and photograph a sample over and over to build a 3D view of infected cells. This guide explains that method and shows that SARS-CoV-2 particles prefer curved patches of the cell surface.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM of a chosen cell inside a millimeter-scale specimen requires targeting based on molecular identity from fluorescence, not blind milling.
ocar.challenge: Precise correlation between fluorescence identity and ultrastructural acquisition is still a workflow bottleneck.
ocar.action: Ronchi, Schwab and colleagues present a high-precision targeting workflow for volume EM so that single cells identified by fluorescence can be visualized ultrastructurally.
ocar.resolution: The method allows ultrastructural visualization of single cells within millimeter-range specimens based on fluorescent molecular identity.
ocar.future_work: The workflow is offered to facilitate targeted vEM acquisitions more generally.

summaries.beginner: Finding one interesting cell in a large sample and then taking an electron-microscope volume of just that cell is tricky. This paper describes a careful targeting recipe that starts from a fluorescent label.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Cell Biology in 2021, Ronchi, Mizzon, Machado, Mahamid, Schwab and colleagues describe a high-precision targeting workflow for volume electron microscopy. Fluorescence-defined molecular identity guides ultrastructural imaging of single cells inside millimeter-scale specimens. The contribution is correlative targeting, not a new microscope.
summaries.advanced: No numeric targeting-error is in the abstract. Catalog method is volume EM; stage is acquisition. Specimen type is generic millimeter-range, not a named connectome volume.

plain_language_summary: Finding one interesting cell in a large sample and then taking an electron-microscope volume of just that cell is tricky. This paper describes a careful targeting recipe that starts from a fluorescent label.

ocar.opportunity: Primate prefrontal cortex is dramatically expanded yet only partly understood in its local and long-distance organization. High-resolution mapping in marmoset can reveal projection motifs that mice may lack.
ocar.challenge: How patchy versus diffuse corticocortical and corticostriatal projections relate to PFC gradients, reciprocal precision, and laminar axonal spread was unclear.
ocar.action: Watakabe, Yamamori and colleagues perform high-resolution connectomic mapping of marmoset PFC, including parcellation-free analyses and mouse comparisons.
ocar.resolution: They find contrasting patchy columnar projections (submillimeter columns in nearby and distant regions) and diffuse projections across cortex and striatum; PFC gradients are represented in local and global projection distributions; reciprocal cortico-cortical connectivity has column-scale precision, suggesting a mosaic of discrete columns. Diffuse axons vary in laminar spread. Columnar projections are much less conspicuous in mice.
ocar.future_work: Findings are offered as principles of primate PFC organization with implications for functional architecture.

summaries.beginner: The front of the primate brain is large and complicated. Mapping marmoset prefrontal connections, this team finds both tight columns of outgoing fibers and wide sprays, a pattern much weaker in mice.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2021/2023 Neuron-linked bioRxiv record, Watakabe, Skibbe, Nakae, Okano, Ishii, Yamamori and colleagues map marmoset prefrontal corticocortical and corticostriatal projections. Patchy submillimeter columns contrast with diffuse axons; gradients appear in projection statistics; reciprocal connections show column-scale precision. Mouse columnar projections are far less conspicuous, underscoring the primate model.
summaries.advanced: This is mesoscale tracing connectomics, not EM. Catalog organism is ‘other’ (marmoset). Catalog year is 2021 with a 2023 Neuron DOI in the record—cite as the marmoset PFC mapping study. ‘Mosaic of discrete columns’ is inferred from reciprocal precision.

plain_language_summary: The front of the primate brain is large and complicated. Mapping marmoset prefrontal connections, this team finds both tight columns of outgoing fibers and wide sprays, a pattern much weaker in mice.

ocar.opportunity: The cerebellar cortex’s regular architecture inspired computational theories, but relating structure, function, and dynamics still needs a reconstruct-and-simulate framework with morphologically realistic neurons.
ocar.challenge: Experimental connectivity data are scattered; unifying them into a coherent connectome and validating against in vivo activity is difficult.
ocar.action: De Schepper, D’Angelo and colleagues reconstruct and simulate mouse cerebellar cortex with multi-compartmental neuron models, generate a connectome via connection rules, and drive the circuit with naturalistic background and sensory-burst stimulation.
ocar.resolution: Simulations show mossy fibers entraining local microcircuits and boosting columns of activity from granular to molecular layer. The model provides model-based ground truth on circuit organization and a resource for local computation and behavioral correlates.
ocar.future_work: The framework is positioned for further investigation of cerebellar computation and behavior.

summaries.beginner: The cerebellum looks like a crystal of repeating circuits, but matching that wiring to real activity is hard. This team built a detailed computer cerebellum for the mouse and watched simulated mossy-fiber input create traveling columns of activity.
summaries.intermediate: In Communications Biology in 2021, De Schepper, Geminiani, Masoli, Rizza, Antonietti, Casellato and D’Angelo reconstruct mouse cerebellar cortex with morphologically realistic multi-compartment models and rule-based connectivity that unifies scattered data. Naturalistic background and sensory-burst stimulation are compared with in vivo recordings. Mossy fibers entrain microcircuits and boost granular-to-molecular activity columns.
summaries.advanced: Connectome generation uses connection rules, not a fully measured EM volume. Validation is against in vivo recordings as stated; quantitative error is not in the abstract. Catalog organism is mouse; stages include infrastructure and modeling.

ocar.opportunity: When new EM stacks are rare or scanning is unstable, a transductive method that labels an entire series from few teacher slices is more appropriate than chasing generalization to unseen samples.
ocar.challenge: Supervised deep segmentation needs many annotations; serial EM’s strong adjacent-slice correlation is underused if each slice is treated independently.
ocar.action: Takaya, Kurihara and colleagues propose sequential semi-supervised segmentation (4S), iterating training, inference, and pseudo-labeling along the stack from a minimal set of teacher labels.
ocar.resolution: On two serial-section image types the method outperformed supervised learning when labels were few. Experiments clarified how the number and position of teacher labels affect performance.
ocar.future_work: They plan to develop 4S as a core module of a general-purpose annotation tool.

summaries.beginner: If you only have time to label a few slices in a long electron-microscope stack, you can still teach a network to fill in the rest by walking from one slice to the next. This paper tests that idea and shows where those few labels should sit.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neuroscience Methods in 2021, Takaya, Takeichi, Ozaki and Kurihara introduce sequential semi-supervised segmentation (4S) for serial EM. Using adjacent-slice correlation, the method iterates train–infer–pseudo-label from few teacher labels in a transductive setting. It beat small-label supervised learning on two serial image types; teacher count and position mattered.
summaries.advanced: The setting explicitly avoids generalization to newly obtained samples. Two image types are unnamed. Catalog stages include sectioning, segmentation, and proofreading; method electron microscopy. Planned annotation-tool integration is future work.

ocar.opportunity: The cortico–basal ganglia–thalamo–cortical loop is a fundamental motif for cognition, sensorimotor behavior, and many disorders, but the classical three-channel (motor, limbic, associative) view cannot explain the basal ganglia’s myriad functions.
ocar.challenge: A finer multi-synaptic map from cortical-defined striatal domains through GPe, SNr, thalamus, and back to cortex was missing.
ocar.action: Foster, Hintiryan, Dong and colleagues map outputs of 29 dorsal-striatal domains (previously defined by cortical input topography) through GPe, SNr, thalamic nuclei, and cortex.
ocar.resolution: They identify 14 SNr and 36 GPe domains and a direct cortico-SNr projection. The direct pathway converges more than the parallel indirect pathway, yet both from the same striatal domain meet on the same postsynaptic SNr neurons. Six parafascicular/ventromedial thalamic domains and six parallel cortico–basal ganglia–thalamic subnetworks form bona fide closed loops back to originating corticostriatal neurons.
ocar.future_work: The mesoscale map is offered as revealing architectural and information-processing features of the loop.

summaries.beginner: A famous brain loop through the basal ganglia was long split into just three channels, which is too coarse. This mouse-tracing study splits the loop into six parallel closed circuits that carry different sets of cortical information all the way around and back.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature in 2021, Foster, Korobkova, Hintiryan, Dong and colleagues map multi-synaptic outputs of 29 cortical-input-defined dorsal striatal domains in mouse. They report 14 substantia nigra reticular and 36 globus pallidus external domains, a direct cortico-nigral projection, and greater convergence on the direct than the indirect pathway, yet common nigral targets. Six thalamic domains close six parallel cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic subnetworks back onto the originating corticostriatal neurons.
summaries.advanced: This is mesoscale tracing, not EM. The 29 striatal domains come from prior cortical-input topography (citation 5 in the abstract). Catalog organism is mouse; method tag ‘Network motifs’ is conceptual. Closed-loop identity is defined by return to originating corticostriatal neurons.
